prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: Across the five frames, the scene is an outdoor work area with a standing man roughly 1.5–2.5 m in front of the camera wearer, while the wearer’s forearm and the green round object move from about 0.5–1 m away to approximately 0.15–0.3 m in frames 3–4, then remain close at the upper right in frame 5. A curved wooden rail lies between or beside the wearer and the man, extending diagonally through the middle distance; the ground and more distant fencing/building surfaces appear progressively darker, supporting their greater depth. In frame 5, another person is partly visible at the far right, approximately 1–2 m away and laterally separated from the central man by roughly 1 m; the central man stays farther away while the wearer’s raised arm occludes part of the scene. The depth map makes near–far ordering and the rapid approach of the hand/object clearer than RGB alone, but it has blurred boundaries, merges nearby limbs with other surfaces, and does not support precise metric distances or reliable detail in the dark background.
descriptions.segmentation: The segmentation map consistently isolates the standing man near the upper-left or upper-middle of each frame and the camera wearer’s arm/hand rising from the lower part of frames 2–5, clarifying which overlapping regions belong to separate people. It shows the wearer’s limb extending to within immediate arm’s reach of the green round object, while the other man remains roughly 1.5–2.5 m ahead; by frame 5, an additional person is partly out of view at the right edge and separated from the central man by about 1 m. Across the strip, the wearer’s arm shifts upward and rightward and increasingly occludes the scene, whereas the standing man changes image position mainly because the camera turns rather than showing a clear large approach or retreat. The masks reveal object/person boundaries that are difficult to follow in RGB, but they are unreliable: parts of the wearer are split into multiple “person” instances, the green object is inconsistently labeled as “frisbee” or “ball,” a background region is mislabeled “surfboard,” and the wooden rail, tools, ground, and many partial objects are omitted.
descriptions.pose: The pose map provides a body skeleton for the standing man in frames 1–2, placing his torso and legs upright ahead of the wearer and showing one arm angled toward the camera-side object; his torso orientation is generally toward the camera wearer, although head and eye direction are too incomplete to establish gaze reliably. Magenta hand landmarks in frame 2 show the wearer’s hand close to and partly overlapping the man’s hand in image space, indicating that both are near the same object and likely within mutual arm’s reach; frame 3 instead shows a large close hand skeleton near the lower centre, consistent with the wearer bringing the object toward the camera. In frame 4 only a small hand cluster remains near the upper centre, and frame 5 contains no reliable skeletons, so turning, approach, retreat, and the additional right-edge person cannot be tracked continuously. The map exposes limb articulation and hand proximity that RGB alone makes hard to separate, but missing joints, disconnected landmarks, severe truncation, and absent detections make depth, gaze, occlusion, and frame-to-frame identity unreliable.
